faqs.a: This tool lists up to 96 individual colors sorted by share - the full inventory. The dominant colors tool distils the same image into a 6-swatch palette. Use this one when you need a specific shade, the other when you want a theme.
faqs.q: How is this different from the dominant colors tool?

faqs.a: Real photos contain gradients, shadows, and JPEG compression noise, so neighbouring pixels almost never match exactly. Flat-design screenshots and logos usually show a short, clean list.
faqs.q: Why does my photo show thousands of unique colors?

faqs.a: They are exact for the 4-bit bucket each pixel lands in. Two shades that differ by less than about 16 steps per channel merge into one swatch, which is why near-identical tones appear as a single color.
The tool reads the RGB values of each pixel. For transparent areas, most browsers report the color after blending against the page background, so treat glassy or faded edges as approximate.

image-color-extractor.formula:
bucket = (R >> 4) << 8 | (G >> 4) << 4 | (B >> 4)
share of color = pixels in bucket / total pixels x 100
Example: a 2x2 image (4 pixels) with 2 red pixels: 2 / 4 x 100 = 50%.

image-color-extractor.quickAnswer: Upload any image and this tool lists its colors from most to least common, each with a HEX and RGB code you can copy in one click. It downsamples the image to at most 160 pixels wide for speed and groups nearly-identical shades into 4,096 buckets. A 2 by 2 image with two red pixels, one blue and one green reports #FF0000 at 50 percent, #0000FF at 25 percent and #00FF00 at 25 percent.
image-color-extractor.tagline: See every color hiding inside any image, with HEX and RGB codes you can copy.
image-color-extractor.workedExample:
Take a tiny 2 by 2 image: two red pixels, one blue pixel, one green pixel.
1. Total pixels sampled: 4.
2. Red bucket: 2 pixels. Share = 2 / 4 x 100 = 50%. HEX #FF0000.
3. Blue bucket: 1 pixel. Share = 1 / 4 x 100 = 25%. HEX #0000FF.
4. Green bucket: 1 pixel. Share = 1 / 4 x 100 = 25%. HEX #00FF00.
5. Sorted by share: #FF0000 (50%), #0000FF (25%), #00FF00 (25%).
That is exactly what the tool reports, just scaled up to real photos.
